Superconductivity in the tt-t′t^{\prime} Hubbard Model from
Symmetry-Preserving Neural-Network Quantum States

August 24, 2026
Abstract

Despite its fundamental importance in the theory of strongly correlated electrons, the nature of the ground state of the two-dimensional doped Hubbard model remains intensely debated. Variational approaches provide a powerful route to this problem, but their conclusions can depend sensitively on the chosen wave-function parameterization, the mean-field initialization, or the pinning fields used to guide the optimization, as well as on boundary conditions. This can favor one type of symmetry breaking over another, making it difficult to distinguish the genuine interplay of intertwined or competing orders from biases induced by the variational parameterization. Here, we introduce the Symmetry-Preserving Backflow Pairing (SBP) ansatz, a neural-network wave function that respects translational symmetry by construction and thereby avoids these broken-symmetry minima. The SBP ansatz reaches state-of-the-art variational energies for the tt-t′t^{\prime} Hubbard model on lattices up to 24×2424\times 24 with 504504 electrons, below those of competing pure stripe solutions. By extrapolating to the thermodynamic limit, we find robust evidence for dd-wave superconducting order, resolving a long-standing question about the 1/81/8-doped model at t′/t=−0.2t^{\prime}/t=-0.2 and U/t=8.0U/t=8.0. Built on general principles of symmetry and locality, the SBP wave function provides a broadly applicable variational representation for challenging interacting fermionic systems.

I Introduction

The two-dimensional Hubbard model is one of the simplest models of strongly correlated electrons, and it is widely regarded as a minimal model that qualitatively captures key physical aspects of the copper-oxide superconductors  [18, 2, 33]. Despite its simple form, its phase diagram at finite doping is still not settled [22]. Antiferromagnetism, charge and spin modulations, and unconventional pairing arise from the same microscopic interaction; the corresponding states are very close in energy, and these intertwined orders [11] can coexist [55, 39]. As a result, different numerical methods have reached different conclusions about which state has the lowest energy [53, 47, 34, 42, 44, 15, 39, 28].

Progress on this problem has been substantial [22], yet a striking feature is that different conclusions are reached not only by different methods but also within the same numerical approach [17, 21, 20]. A recent large-scale study combining density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) with constrained-path auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) reports that, when the next-nearest-neighbor hopping t′t^{\prime} is negative, superconductivity coexists with partially filled stripes [55], whereas a separate DMRG study finds no superconductivity for t′<0t^{\prime}<0 and remains inconclusive about its presence for t′>0t^{\prime}>0 [20]. A similar situation arises for Neural-Network Quantum States (NQS) [6]. A wave function built from backflow determinants finds only pure stripe order [15, 14], while a Pfaffian-based wave function reports clear signatures of superconductivity for t′<0t^{\prime}<0 and even evidence for superconductivity in the pure Hubbard model at t′=0t^{\prime}=0 [39]. A likely origin of these discrepancies is that each numerical method carries its own bias, mainly through the boundary conditions and the lattice geometries in tensor network-based approaches [17, 21, 25, 20] and through the initial mean-field state used to initialize the optimization [39] or the specific functional form of the variational state in NQS [51].

In this work, we focus on the paradigmatic tt-t′t^{\prime} Hubbard model, whose Hamiltonian reads

H^=−t∑⟨i​j⟩,σc^†i​σc^j​σ−t′∑⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩,σc^†i​σc^j​σ+U∑in^i↑n^i↓,\hat{H}=-t\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,\sigma}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}\hat{c}_{j\sigma}-t^{\prime}\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle,\sigma}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}\hat{c}_{j\sigma}+U\sum_{i}\hat{n}_{i\uparrow}\hat{n}_{i\downarrow}\ , (1)

where ii and jj label the sites of the lattice, c^i​σ†\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{i\sigma} (c^i​σ\hat{c}_{i\sigma}) creates (annihilates) an electron with spin σ={↑,↓}\sigma=\{\uparrow,\downarrow\} on site ii, and n^i​σ=c^i​σ†​c^i​σ\hat{n}_{i\sigma}=\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}\hat{c}_{i\sigma} is the number operator. The sums ⟨i​j⟩\langle ij\rangle and ⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle run over nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor pairs, with hopping amplitudes tt and t′t^{\prime}, while UU is the on-site repulsion. We set t=1.0t=1.0 as the unit of energy and take t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2 and U=8.0U=8.0 in order to compare with previous works [55, 20]. These values are in the range relevant to cuprate superconductors, with |t′/t||t^{\prime}/t| varying from ∼0.15\sim 0.15 to ∼0.4\sim 0.4 depending on the compound  [1, 16, 40]. We study L×LL\times L square lattices (N=L2N=L^{2}) with periodic boundary conditions and a number of electrons Ne=N⁡(1−δ)N_{e}=N(1-\delta) chosen such that the doping level is fixed to δ=1/8\delta=1/8.

The most common fermionic NQS parametrizations are based on backflow determinants [27], and they often converge to states that break the symmetries of the Hamiltonian, even in the presence of periodic boundary conditions. In the Hubbard model, these solutions typically display charge and spin stripe patterns that break translational symmetry [15, 14, 58, 29, 41, 59, 23, 19, 9].

In this work, we first demonstrate this behavior explicitly: when the variational manifold allows broken translational symmetry solutions, the optimization readily converges to several distinct pure stripe states with competitive variational energies. In the tt-t′t^{\prime} Hubbard model [see Eq. 1], this is a serious limitation because broken-symmetry solutions can display physical properties that differ markedly from those of the symmetric state, typically suppressing pairing correlations and leading to states with weak or absent superconducting order - see Ref. [51] for a detailed discussion. We expect that a related mechanism may also affect DMRG and other related tensor-network approaches, where cylindrical geometries and open boundary conditions naturally favor the stabilization of pure stripe patterns [25, 57]. In addition, such pure stripe states may be represented more efficiently at finite bond dimension than superconducting states, an interpretation consistent with Ref. [20], where superconducting correlations are found to be underestimated at finite bond dimension.

On a finite cluster with periodic boundary conditions, a broken-symmetry state can be an exact ground state only in the presence of degeneracy, whereas when the Hamiltonian has symmetries, its exact eigenstates can always be chosen to transform according to definite irreducible representations of the symmetry group [54]. Targeting the symmetric state directly, however, is not straightforward, since constructing expressive variational states that preserve translational symmetry by construction can be more challenging. Indeed, several works have shown that the most accurate variational results are often obtained by first allowing the wave function to break the symmetries of the Hamiltonian and then restoring them a posteriori through quantum-number projection [35, 45, 31]. In the Hubbard model, however, the presence of competing pure stripe states makes this strategy effective only on relatively small system sizes [51], as discussed below.

In order to overcome these problems, we propose the Symmetry-Preserving Backflow Pairing (SBP) wave function that is designed to respect the translational symmetry of the Hamiltonian and, unlike previous constructions [15, 14], does not become trapped in the local minima associated with broken-symmetry solutions of spin or charge. By enforcing the relevant symmetries at the level of the variational parametrization, the ansatz appears to reshape the optimization landscape into an effectively “convex” one: starting from different random initializations, the optimization converges to different sets of parameters that nonetheless describe the same physical state, with compatible energy and correlation functions; see Fig. 1 for a pictorial illustration. This behavior is consistent with the overparametrized regime typical of deep learning, where distinct sets of parameters can represent the same function and the minima reached from different initializations are effectively equivalent [24, 13, 10]. In practice, this means that the basin of attraction of the minimum corresponding to the lowest variational energy is enlarged when considering a symmetric ansatz, making the landscape more convex in its vicinity - while other local minima outside this basin can of course still exist.

Our method reaches state-of-the-art variational energies, lower than those of competing pure stripe solutions on the same clusters, for lattices up to 24×2424\times 24 and 504504 electrons. By extrapolating the superconducting order parameter to the thermodynamic limit, we find strong numerical evidence for robust dd-wave superconductivity.

These results address a fundamental long-standing question about the nature of the ground state of the 1/81/8-doped model Hubbard model at t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2 and U=8.0U=8.0, a parameter range relevant to cuprate superconductors.

II Symmetry-Preserving Backflow Pairing

We introduce the Symmetry-Preserving Backflow Pairing (SBP) ansatz, a generalization of the pair-product wave function [30, 45, 19, 9]. The variational state Ψθ​(𝒏)\Psi_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{n}), with θ\theta a set of parameters, takes as input a physical configuration 𝒏=(n1↑,…,nN↑,n1↓,…,nN↓){\boldsymbol{n}=(n_{1\uparrow},\ldots,n_{N\uparrow},n_{1\downarrow},\ldots,n_{N\downarrow})}, encoded as a binary string of occupations ni​σ∈{0,1}n_{i\sigma}\in\{0,1\}. The wave function is defined as

Ψθ​(𝒏)=⟨𝒏|(∑i,j=1Nfi​j​(𝒏)​ci↑†​cj↓†)Ne/2|0⟩,\Psi_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{n})=\langle\boldsymbol{n}|\left(\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}f_{ij}(\boldsymbol{n})\,c^{\dagger}_{i\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{j\downarrow}\right)^{N_{e}/2}|0\rangle, (2)

where NeN_{e} is the number of electrons and f⁡(𝒏)f(\boldsymbol{n}) is a configuration-dependent N×NN\times N pairing matrix generated by the neural network. Since the backflow pairing orbitals only connect up and down spins [see Eq. 2], the amplitude can be evaluated as a determinant instead of a Pfaffian [45, 5]:

Ψθ​(𝒏)=det[𝒏↑⋆f⁡(𝒏)⋆𝒏↓],\Psi_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{n})=\det[\,\boldsymbol{n}_{\uparrow}\star f(\boldsymbol{n})\star\boldsymbol{n}_{\downarrow}\,], (3)

where 𝒏↑⋆f⁡(𝒏)⋆𝒏↓\boldsymbol{n}_{\uparrow}\star f(\boldsymbol{n})\star\boldsymbol{n}_{\downarrow} denotes the Ne/2×Ne/2N_{e}/2\times N_{e}/2 submatrix of f⁡(𝒏)f(\boldsymbol{n}) obtained by retaining only the rows and columns corresponding to occupied up- and down-spin sites, respectively. This formulation allows the spatial symmetries of the Hamiltonian to be incorporated directly through the parametrization of f⁡(𝒏)f(\boldsymbol{n}).

In this work, we introduce the following backflow form for the pairing matrix [26, 8, 51]:

fi​j​(𝒏)=e−λ​d​(i,j)∑i′​j′e−λ​d​(i′,j′)​∑α=1dWi−j,α​yi​α↑​(𝒏)​yj​α↓​(𝒏),f_{ij}(\boldsymbol{n})=\frac{e^{-\lambda d(i,j)}}{\sum_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}e^{-\lambda d(i^{\prime},j^{\prime})}}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{d}W_{i-j,\,\alpha}\,y^{\uparrow}_{i\alpha}(\boldsymbol{n})\,y^{\downarrow}_{j\alpha}(\boldsymbol{n})\ , (4)

where the backflow transformation produces the dd-dimensional vectors yiσ​(𝒏)y^{\sigma}_{i}(\boldsymbol{n}), which provide an abstract, configuration-dependent representation of the input configuration 𝒏\boldsymbol{n}. These vectors are generated by a translationally equivariant transformer-based architecture [49, 50], additional details are given in the Methods. The matrix of Wi−j,αW_{i-j,\alpha} depends only on the relative displacement i−ji-j to preserve translational symmetry: this results in N×dN\times d independent trainable parameters. For square geometries, the C4​vC_{4v} point-group symmetry can also be incorporated explicitly into the variational state (see Methods). Since this group has only eight elements, however, we restore it a posteriori by quantum-number projection [45, 37].

The prefactor e−λ​d​(i,j)/∑i′​j′e−λ​d​(i′,j′)e^{-\lambda d(i,j)}/\sum_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}e^{-\lambda d(i^{\prime},j^{\prime})} in Eq. 4 introduces a spatial decay in the pairing matrix. This choice is motivated by the physical interpretation of fi​j​(𝒏)f_{ij}(\boldsymbol{n}) as the amplitude for creating a pair of electrons on sites ii and jj, with spins ↑\uparrow and ↓\downarrow, respectively. For a local Hamiltonian, such amplitudes are expected to decay with the distance between the two sites, independently of the configuration 𝒏\boldsymbol{n}. We emphasize that the locality of the pairing amplitude fi​jf_{ij} does not imply short-range pairing correlations, as illustrated for example by the attractive Hubbard model, where a local pairing amplitude gives rise to off-diagonal long-range order. Here d⁡(i,j)d(i,j) is the Euclidean distance between sites ii and jj on the lattice, and λ>0\lambda>0 is a trainable parameter controlling the decay length. The denominator normalizes the weights over all pairs. In this way, the ansatz suppresses matrix elements between distant sites of the pairing matrix while allowing the optimization to determine the appropriate decay scale. This bias becomes important for large lattices; it stabilizes the optimization, speeds up convergence, and drives it to lower energy solutions. A related spatial bias has originally been used in the transformer attention mechanism to obtain stable and accurate optimization on large spin systems on lattice [52] and more recently in electronic systems in continuous space [12].

III Symmetry breaking and local minima

In this Section, we provide evidence for the presence of distinct local minima in the variational landscape when using variational wave functions that explicitly break lattice symmetries. To this end, we introduce a parametrization of the pairing matrix in Eq. 2 that does not enforce translational symmetry. Following the construction of the backflow Pfaffian output layer introduced in Refs. [8, 26, 51], we define

fi​j​(𝒏)=∑α=1dΦi​α↑​(𝒏)​Φj​α↓​(𝒏).f_{ij}(\boldsymbol{n})=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{d}\Phi^{\uparrow}_{i\alpha}(\boldsymbol{n})\ \Phi^{\downarrow}_{j\alpha}(\boldsymbol{n}). (5)

where Φi​ασ\Phi^{\sigma}_{i\alpha} are backflow orbitals obtained through a site-resolved linear mapping of the transformer outputs, namely Φi​ασ​(𝒏)=∑β=1dWi​α​βσ​yi​βσ​(𝒏){\Phi^{\sigma}_{i\alpha}(\boldsymbol{n})=\sum_{\beta=1}^{d}W^{\sigma}_{i\alpha\beta}\ y^{\sigma}_{i\beta}}(\boldsymbol{n}). In the following, we refer to this state as the Backflow Pairing (BP) ansatz.

In Fig. 2, we compare the optimization of the symmetry-preserving backflow-pairing state, denoted as SBP and defined in Eq. 4, with that of the BP state in Eq. 5. Figure 2(a) shows the variational energy per site as a function of the optimization step. The SBP state converges rapidly and reaches the lowest energy, whereas the two BP optimizations converge more slowly to higher energies. Crucially, the two SBP runs, initialized with different random seeds, converge to the same energy, whereas the final energies of the two BP runs depend on the random seed used to initialize the variational parameters. This shows that the BP optimization is trapped in distinct local minima, while the SBP ansatz reliably reaches the same solution regardless of initialization. We stress that our goal here is not to find the lowest-energy pure stripe state, but to demonstrate that explicitly breaking translational symmetry gives rise to multiple pure stripe solutions. The best pure stripe variational energies available in the literature [15, 14] are reported in Table 1.

To quantify the emergence of symmetry breaking during the optimization, we introduce the quantities:

δn2=∑i=1N(⟨n^i⟩−n0)2,δs2=∑i=1N⟨S^iz⟩2.\delta^{2}_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\langle\hat{n}_{i}\rangle-n_{0}\right)^{2},\qquad\delta^{2}_{s}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\langle\hat{S}^{z}_{i}\rangle^{2}. (6)

Here, n0=Ne/Nn_{0}=N_{\mathrm{e}}/N is the density. The quantities δn\delta_{n} and δs\delta_{s} measure the amplitude of spatial modulations in the local density and in the local magnetization, respectively. Figure 2(b) and Fig. 2(c) show their evolution during the optimization. For the SBP ansatz, both remain very small and constant throughout the entire optimization, so the state remains translationally invariant with no spatial modulation of the local spin moment or charge density. For the BP, instead, δs\delta_{s} and δn\delta_{n} grow to finite values, showing that the optimization is driven toward broken-symmetry solutions with pure stripe ordering.

To characterize the broken-symmetry solutions reached by the BP ansatz, in Fig. 3 we show the local charge density ⟨n^i⟩\langle\hat{n}_{i}\rangle and the local magnetization ⟨S^iz⟩\langle\hat{S}^{z}_{i}\rangle for the two solutions obtained from the random seeds used in Fig. 2. The color of each site encodes the charge density, as indicated by the color bar, while the arrows show the magnitude and sign of the local spin polarization. In both cases, the local observables are not uniform across the lattice but display clear spatial modulations. We emphasize that this behavior does not stem from a lack of expressivity of the BP parametrization: the state in Eq. 5 can also represent the translationally invariant solution of the SBP ansatz in Eq. 4, but in practice, this solution is difficult to reach through unconstrained optimization.

Crucially, as shown in Ref. [51], these broken-symmetry solutions typically display weak or no superconductivity. One possible strategy to stabilize the superconducting solution would be to restore translational symmetry a posteriori by quantum-number projection [51, 45, 31]. However, this becomes increasingly expensive with system size, as the projected wave function requires a sum over all translations, whose number grows with the number of lattice sites. The limitation may not be only computational: when the optimized state is strongly trapped in a broken-symmetry minimum, the translated configurations can have small overlap with the original one, which may hinder the optimization. Symmetry restoration is therefore effective on small clusters but impractical on large ones [51].

The occurrence of multiple stripe solutions is also observed in tensor-network approaches [25], where open boundary conditions favor stripe order, and pinning fields are often introduced to stabilize specific patterns [57, 25]. Similar behavior has also been reported in neural-network approaches; for example, Ref. [15] compares different stripe solutions and measures the energy difference between horizontal and vertical stripes. This contrasts with the SBP ansatz in Eq. 4, for which the final solutions share the same energy and physical properties regardless of the random initialization of the parameters: in this case, the landscape appears to be effectively “convex” [24, 13, 10] within the basin of attraction of the lowest energy variational state.

IV Results

The SBP wave function achieves state-of-the-art variational results for the tt-t′t^{\prime} Hubbard model. In Table 1, we report the variational energies per site for 12×1212\times 12, 16×1616\times 16, 20×2020\times 20, and 24×2424\times 24 square lattices with periodic boundary conditions, together with the best available results in the literature. For a fair comparison, we include only energies obtained by direct variational optimization, excluding additional projector improvements such as Green Function Monte Carlo (GFMC) [48, 46] or Lanczos steps [4]. These techniques can be applied a posteriori to any optimized variational state and systematically lower the energy, but usually without inducing significant changes in its physical properties [19]. On any system size, the SBP wave function reaches an energy that is lower than all previous variational results. Moreover, since the SBP variational state is translationally invariant, it is scalable across lattice sizes, and we can apply a transfer-learning procedure in which the wave function optimized on the 20×2020\times 20 lattice is used as the starting point for the 24×2424\times 24 lattice. In this way, the energy on the 24×2424\times 24 lattice is obtained with 20002000 GPU hours on NVIDIA H200 nodes.

Beyond the variational energy, the physical properties of the tt-t′t^{\prime} Hubbard model at finite doping remain under debate: antiferromagnetism, charge and spin modulations, and unconventional pairing all compete or coexist. Different numerical methods have reached different conclusions about whether superconductivity is present and whether it coexists with stripe order [57, 19, 9, 21, 32, 44, 55, 39, 51]. Here, we provide strong numerical evidence of the presence of dd-wave superconductivity in the 1/81/8-doped model at t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2 and U=8.0U=8.0, on large system sizes through the long distance behavior of the pairing correlation function [32, 39, 51]:

Cp​(r)=18​∑η,η′h0,η​hr,η′​⟨c^η,↓†​c^0,↑†​c^r,↑​c^r+η′,↓⟩−𝒩0,r,C_{p}(r)=\frac{1}{8}\sum_{\eta,\eta^{\prime}}h_{0,\eta}h_{r,\eta^{\prime}}\left\langle\hat{c}_{\eta,\downarrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{0,\uparrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{r,\uparrow}\hat{c}_{r+\eta^{\prime},\downarrow}\right\rangle-\mathcal{N}_{0,r}\ , (7)

the sum over η\eta runs over the four nearest neighbors of rr, and hr,η=+1h_{r,\eta}=+1 on horizontal bonds and hr,η=−1h_{r,\eta}=-1 on vertical bonds, so that the pair carries symmetry dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}. The numerical prefactors in the definitions of Cp​(r)C_{p}(r) is chosen so that its long-distance behavior can be directly compared with the standard convention used in Refs. [32, 55]. The term 𝒩0,r\mathcal{N}_{0,r} subtracts the disconnected contribution [39]. Refer to Methods for additional details.

A finite value of Cp​(r)C_{p}(r) at large distances signals superconducting dd-wave order. In Fig. 4 we show Cp​(r)C_{p}(r) as a function of distance |r||r|. After a fast decay at short distances, the correlation function saturates to a finite value as |r||r| grows. The inset of Fig. 4 shows the dd-wave order parameter [19]

ΔSC2=1ℳ​∑|r|≥rmaxCp​(|r|),\Delta^{2}_{\mathrm{SC}}=\frac{1}{\mathcal{M}}\sum_{|r|\geq r_{\max}}C_{p}(|r|)\ , (8)

which averages the pairing correlation function over the saturation region |r|≥rmax|r|\geq r_{\max}, with rmax=dmax/2r_{\max}=d_{\max}/2 (where dmaxd_{\max} is the largest distance between two sites of the L×LL\times L cluster) and ℳ\mathcal{M} the number of such vectors. We plot ΔSC\Delta_{\mathrm{SC}} as a function of 1/L1/L, together with the reference value of Ref. [55], obtained with constrained-path auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC). The extrapolation to 1/L→01/L\to 0 yields a finite value, ΔSC=0.022​(1)\Delta_{\mathrm{SC}}=0.022(1), in agreement with the previous estimate within error bars.

We note that the result of Ref. [55] was obtained on cylindrical geometries, with open boundary conditions along the long direction, by introducing an external pairing field [55, 32] and averaging over twisted boundary conditions. Here, instead, we obtain a consistent value by considering only square clusters with periodic boundary conditions and measuring the superconducting order parameter directly from the long-distance behavior of correlation functions. Extracting the thermodynamic properties of the Hubbard model from large square clusters with periodic boundary conditions marks a methodological advance for the numerical study of strongly correlated fermions.

In Fig. 5 we show the spin-spin correlation function Cs​(r)=⟨𝑺^0⋅𝑺^r⟩C_{s}(r)=\langle\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{0}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{r}\rangle for a 24×2424\times 24 lattice. The correlations follow an antiferromagnetic pattern, modulated by a longer-wavelength stripe envelope [34, 39, 21], so that stripe order is clearly present on this cluster. Whether this modulation survives in the thermodynamic limit and long-range stripe order coexists with superconductivity, or whether these stripe correlations only exist over intermediate scales is a computationally delicate issue which should be addressed in future work. Because the SBP wave function is translationally invariant, the physics of stripes is revealed only by the correlation function and not by the one-body observables [51]: the local quantity ⟨S^iz⟩\langle\hat{S}^{z}_{i}\rangle remains uniform across the lattice, as mentioned above, in contrast to the broken-symmetry solutions of Fig. 3.

V Discussion

In variational optimization, the structure of the energy landscape is determined both by the Hamiltonian and by the functional form of the wave function. As a consequence, the choice of ansatz controls which regions of the variational manifold can be efficiently explored and which minima are most easily reached during training. For the tt-t′t^{\prime} Hubbard model, we have shown that wave functions that explicitly break translational invariance generate a landscape with several competing local minima associated with distinct broken-symmetry pure stripe patterns that typically display weak or no superconducting order [51].

To address this, we introduced the Symmetry-Preserving Backflow Pairing, or SBP, wave function, which enforces translational invariance by construction and removes these symmetry-broken solutions from the accessible variational landscape. Independently of the initialization of the neural-network parameters, the SBP ansatz reaches state-of-the-art variational energies and converges to solutions with consistent physical properties. Moreover, because of its translationally invariant structure, the optimized wave function can be transferred from a given system size to a larger one, leading to a substantial reduction of the computational cost on large systems.

Using the SBP wave function, we computed the ground state of system sizes up to 24×2424\times 24 with 504504 electrons, which were previously out of reach for the tt-t′t^{\prime} Hubbard model using variational neural-network approaches. Our results provide robust evidence that the tt-t′t^{\prime} Hubbard model at t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2, U=8.0U=8.0, and doping δ=1/8\delta=1/8 supports superconducting order, thereby resolving a long-standing question about this parameter regime.

A natural direction for future work is to extend these calculations to other dopings and interaction strengths in order to clarify the ground-state phase diagram of the Hubbard model and, in particular, the interplay between superconductivity and stripes [55]. On the methodological side, a natural extension is to replace the pair-product form of Eq. 2, where pairing is restricted to opposite-spin components, with a more general and expressive Pfaffian parametrization [8, 39, 51]. This would allow the variational state to capture more general pairing structures and could be crucial for obtaining accurate ground states in regions of the phase diagram where different orders are strongly intertwined [19, 9]. More broadly, since the SBP ansatz is based on physically motivated principles rather than being tailored to a specific model, we expect it to provide a powerful and flexible tool for the study of strongly correlated fermionic systems, such as realistic multi-band models of superconductors involving several orbitals per unit cell.

VI Methods

VI.1 Comparison with Quantum Monte Carlo at half filling

To validate the SBP state, we benchmark it against numerically exact results for the pure Hubbard model (t′=0.0CLOSE(t^{\prime}=0.0, OPENU=4.0)U=4.0) at half filling (Ne=N)(N_{e}=N) on a square lattice with periodic boundary conditions. In this regime, the model is free of the sign problem, so quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) provides exact reference data against which the variational results can be compared [34]. Moreover, this case probes the complementary physical regime to the doped case: at half filling, the ground state exhibits strong antiferromagnetic order and no superconductivity. We compute the spin-spin correlation function Cs​(r)=⟨𝑺^0⋅𝑺^r⟩C_{s}(r)=\langle\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{0}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{r}\rangle with the SBP ansatz and compare it with the QMC result of Ref. [34] on a 16×1616\times 16 lattice. The real-space spin-spin correlation functions Cs​(r)C_{s}(r), shown in Fig. 6(c), display the expected antiferromagnetic checkerboard structure, without the longer-wavelength stripe modulation observed in the doped case. As shown in Fig. 6(a), the variational results agree with QMC over the full range of distances, demonstrating that the SBP wave function quantitatively captures the antiferromagnetic correlations of the half-filled model. We then compute the dd-wave pairing correlation function Cp​(r)C_{p}(r) defined above. As shown in panel (b) of Fig. 6, in contrast to the doped case, Cp​(r)C_{p}(r) decays rapidly to very low values, compatible with a state with no dd-wave superconducting order in the thermodynamic limit.

VI.2 Spin correlations in the pure Hubbard model at finite doping

To further assess the ability of the SBP wave function to capture the physics of different parameter regimes, we consider the pure Hubbard model (t′=0.0t^{\prime}=0.0) at U=8.0U=8.0 and doping δ=1/8\delta=1/8 on a 20×2020\times 20 lattice. In Fig. 7, we show the corresponding real-space spin-spin correlation function Cs​(r)C_{s}(r). As in the t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2 case of Fig. 5, the correlations display an antiferromagnetic pattern modulated by a stripe envelope; however, two clear differences emerge. First, the period of the stripe modulation is longer at t′=0.0t^{\prime}=0.0, in agreement with previous studies at this doping [56, 57, 21, 32], whereas at t′=−0.2t^{\prime}=-0.2 the modulation is shorter, consistent with the partially filled stripes reported e.g. in Refs.[55, 20, 39]. Second, the magnitude of the spin-spin correlations at large distances is significantly larger at t′=0t^{\prime}=0, indicating that magnetic order is more robust in the pure Hubbard model. Both features are consistent with the established picture in which a negative t′t^{\prime} frustrates and weakens stripe order, shortening its period and partially melting the magnetic correlations. We stress that since the SBP wave function is translationally invariant, these modulations appear only in the correlation functions, while the one-body observables remain uniform across the lattice.

VI.3 Pairing correlation function

We define the dd-wave spin-singlet pair operator consistent with Refs. [32, 55] as

Δ^r=14​∑ηhr,η​(c^r↑​c^r+η,↓−c^r↓​c^r+η,↑)2,\hat{\Delta}_{r}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\eta}h_{r,\eta}\frac{\left(\hat{c}_{r\uparrow}\hat{c}_{r+\eta,\downarrow}-\hat{c}_{r\downarrow}\hat{c}_{r+\eta,\uparrow}\right)}{\sqrt{2}}\ , (9)

the sum over η\eta runs over the four nearest neighbors of rr, and hr,η=+1h_{r,\eta}=+1 on horizontal bonds and hr,η=−1h_{r,\eta}=-1 on vertical bonds, so that the pair carries symmetry dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}. The corresponding pairing correlation function between the origin and a generic lattice site rr is C⁡(r)=⟨Δ^0†​Δ^r⟩C(r)=\langle\hat{\Delta}^{\dagger}_{0}\hat{\Delta}_{r}\rangle. Expanding the singlet operators gives

C⁡(r)=\displaystyle C(r)= 132∑η,η′h0,ηhr,η′[⟨c^η,↓†c^0,↑†c^r,↑c^r+η′,↓⟩−⟨c^η,↓†c^0,↑†c^r,↓c^r+η′,↑⟩\displaystyle\frac{1}{32}\sum_{\eta,\eta^{\prime}}h_{0,\eta}h_{r,\eta^{\prime}}\Big[\langle\hat{c}_{\eta,\downarrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{0,\uparrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{r,\uparrow}\hat{c}_{r+\eta^{\prime},\downarrow}\rangle-\langle\hat{c}_{\eta,\downarrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{0,\uparrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{r,\downarrow}\hat{c}_{r+\eta^{\prime},\uparrow}\rangle
−⟨c^η,↑†c^0,↓†c^r,↑c^r+η′,↓⟩+⟨c^η,↑†c^0,↓†c^r,↓c^r+η′,↑⟩].\displaystyle-\langle\hat{c}_{\eta,\uparrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{0,\downarrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{r,\uparrow}\hat{c}_{r+\eta^{\prime},\downarrow}\rangle+\langle\hat{c}_{\eta,\uparrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{0,\downarrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{r,\downarrow}\hat{c}_{r+\eta^{\prime},\uparrow}\rangle\Big]\ . (10)

At large separations, spin-singlet superconducting off-diagonal long-range order implies that the four spin-resolved contributions become equivalent once their explicit signs are taken into account. For computational efficiency, we therefore retain only one of them and define

Cp​(r)=18​∑η,η′h0,η​hr,η′​⟨c^η,↓†​c^0,↑†​c^r,↑​c^r+η′,↓⟩−𝒩0,r,C_{p}(r)=\frac{1}{8}\sum_{\eta,\eta^{\prime}}h_{0,\eta}h_{r,\eta^{\prime}}\left\langle\hat{c}_{\eta,\downarrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{0,\uparrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{r,\uparrow}\hat{c}_{r+\eta^{\prime},\downarrow}\right\rangle-\mathcal{N}_{0,r}\ , (11)

where 𝒩0,r=18​∑η,η′h0,η​hr,η′​⟨c^η,↓†​c^r+η′,↓⟩​⟨c^0,↑†​c^r,↑⟩\mathcal{N}_{0,r}=\frac{1}{8}\sum_{\eta,\eta^{\prime}}h_{0,\eta}h_{r,\eta^{\prime}}\langle\hat{c}_{\eta,\downarrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{r+\eta^{\prime},\downarrow}\rangle\langle\hat{c}_{0,\uparrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{r,\uparrow}\rangle is the disconnected contribution, retaining only the contraction that conserves both particle number and total SzS^{z} [39]. This subtraction does not affect the asymptotic value in the thermodynamic limit. The two definitions need not coincide at finite separation, but with the normalization above C​(r)→Cp​(r)C(r)\rightarrow C_{p}(r) as |r|→∞|r|\rightarrow\infty.

VI.4 Transformer architecture and optimization protocol

The transformer architecture processes the input configurations 𝒏=(n0↑,…,nN−1↑,n0↓,…,nN−1↓){\boldsymbol{n}=(n_{0\uparrow},\ldots,n_{N-1\uparrow},n_{0\downarrow},\ldots,n_{N-1\downarrow})} by linearly embedding each local occupation niσn^{\sigma}_{i} into a dd-dimensional vector space, producing the sequence (x0↑,…,xN−1↑,x0↓,…,xN−1↓){(x^{\uparrow}_{0},\dots,x^{\uparrow}_{N-1},x^{\downarrow}_{0},\dots,x^{\downarrow}_{N-1})} with xiσ∈ℝdx^{\sigma}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. This sequence is processed by a stack of layers, each combining a factored self-attention mechanism [38, 36] with spatial bias [52] and a fully connected network. The resulting output sequence (y0↑,…,yN−1↑,y0↓,…,yN−1↓){(y^{\uparrow}_{0},\dots,y^{\uparrow}_{N-1},y^{\downarrow}_{0},\dots,y^{\downarrow}_{N-1})}, with yiσ∈ℝdy_{i}^{\sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, enters the output layer of Eq. 4 to produce the backflow pairing orbitals of the SBP wave function. A detailed description of the transformer architecture and its hyperparameters is given in Refs. [50, 49]. Here we use nl=8n_{l}=8 layers, h=12h=12 heads, and an embedding dimension of d=72d=72. To accelerate the optimization of dd-wave superconducting correlations, we seed the singlet dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} pairing channel by adding to f⁡(𝒏)f(\boldsymbol{n}) [see Eq. 4] a configuration-independent matrix fdf_{d}. Its only nonzero entries connect opposite spins on nearest-neighbor bonds and are defined by (fd)r,r+η=Δd​hr,η(f_{d})_{{r},{r}+{\eta}}=\Delta_{d}\,h_{{r},{\eta}}, where Δd\Delta_{d} is a trainable scalar parameter and hr,η=+1h_{{r},{\eta}}=+1 (hr,η=−1h_{{r},{\eta}}=-1) for η=±x^{\eta}=\pm\hat{{x}} (η=±y^{\eta}=\pm\hat{{y}}). We numerically check that this additional term only improves the learning speed; the final optimized results are independent of whether it is included.

The wave function is optimized within the Variational Monte Carlo framework [3] with Stochastic Reconfiguration [43], using the linear-algebra identity of Refs. [37, 7] and the MARCH optimizer [15]. This identity is convenient in our setup, where the number of samples M=12288{M=12288} is much smaller than the number of parameters P≈5×105{P\approx 5\times 10^{5}}, as it reduces the size of the linear system to be solved from P×PP\times P to M×MM\times M [37].

After the optimization of the SBP wave function [see Eq. 2] we apply quantum number projection [45] to restore the rotational C4​vC_{4v} symmetry [50, 37]. Specifically for the 12×1212\times 12 and 16×1616\times 16 clusters, we optimize for 2×1032\times 10^{3} steps after the symmetry restoration; however, for the 20×2020\times 20 and 24×2424\times 24 clusters, we only perform the sampling without optimization.
